title: Book III: Waiting For Death — Chapter XXVIII
paragraphs:
1_st Gent_. All times are good to seek your wedded home
Bringing a mutual delight.

2_d Gent_. Why, true.
The calendar hath not an evil day
For souls made one by love, and even death
Were sweetness, if it came like rolling waves
While they two clasped each other, and foresaw
No life apart.

Mr. and Mrs. Casaubon came home to Lowick Manor from their wedding journey in mid-January. A little snow was falling as they stepped down at the door. Next morning, when Dorothea left her dressing room for the blue-green sitting room we have seen before, the long avenue of lime trees rose from white ground, spreading white branches beneath a dark, unmoving sky. The flat distance seemed to contract into an unbroken whiteness under an equally unbroken low cloud. Even the room’s furniture appeared smaller than on her first visit. The stag in the tapestry looked more ghostly than ever in its spectral blue-green surroundings; the volumes of elegant literature in the bookcase seemed like fixed imitations of books. Dry oak branches flamed brightly above the logs, bringing an incongruous return of warmth and life—much as Dorothea herself did when she entered with the red leather cases of cameos for Celia.

Fresh from dressing, she glowed with the radiance possible only in healthy youth. Her coiled hair and hazel eyes shone like jewels, and her lips were warm with living color. Above the different whiteness of her fur, her white throat rose and fell with her breathing. The fur seemed to curl around her neck and cling to her blue-gray outer dress with a tenderness borrowed from her own nature, an innocent mingling of living warmth and softness that held its beauty beside the crystalline purity of the snow outside. She placed the cameo cases on the table in the bay window and, without noticing, left her hands resting on them. Her attention had already gone to the still white enclosure that bounded everything she could see.

Mr. Casaubon had risen early, complaining of a pounding heart. He was in the library receiving his curate, Mr. Tucker. Celia would come later, as both sister and bridesmaid. In the weeks ahead there would be wedding visits to receive and return, prolonging that transitional period supposed to match a bride’s excited happiness. They would sustain the feeling of being busy without accomplishing anything, like a dream whose dreamer is starting to suspect it. The duties of marriage, which Dorothea had imagined so momentous, seemed to contract along with the furniture and the landscape walled in by white mist. The clear heights where she had expected to walk in perfect understanding with her husband were becoming hard even to imagine. Instead of the delicious peace of resting her soul on someone wholly superior, she experienced anxious effort disturbed by vague foreboding. When would her days of active, devoted wifehood begin, strengthening his life and lifting hers? Perhaps never in the form she had pictured. Yet somehow—somehow they must. Within this union to which she had solemnly pledged her life, duty would arrive with some fresh inspiration and give a new meaning to a wife’s love.

For now, there were only the snow and the low arch of dark mist. There was the suffocating confinement of a lady’s world, where everything was done for her and nobody needed her help. Any connection with the varied, fertile life beyond it had to be painfully maintained as a private vision, instead of reaching her through demands that could give her energy a purpose. “What should I do?” “Whatever you like, my dear.” That exchange summed up her life since she had stopped having morning lessons and practicing foolish rhythms on the piano she hated. Marriage was supposed to direct her toward worthwhile, necessary work. It had not yet released her from a lady’s oppressive freedom, nor even filled her empty hours with the quiet happiness of tenderness freely given. Her vigorous, flourishing youth stood imprisoned in a life whose confinement merged with the cold, colorless, narrowing view, the diminished furniture, the unread books, and the ghostly stag in its pale, fantastic world, fading out of daylight.

For the first few minutes at the window, Dorothea felt only this bleak oppression. Then a sharp memory came to her. She turned away and walked around the room. The hopes and ideas that had filled her on her first visit, nearly three months earlier, survived now only as memories. She judged them as we judge passing things that have already gone. The whole world seemed to have a weaker pulse than hers. Her religious faith was a lonely cry, an attempt to escape a nightmare in which everything withered and shrank away. Each familiar object had lost its magic, as lifeless as a painted transparency with no light behind it. At last her wandering eyes reached the miniatures. Here, finally, something had gained new life and meaning: the portrait of Mr. Casaubon’s aunt Julia, the woman who had made an unhappy marriage, Will Ladislaw’s grandmother. Dorothea could almost believe the delicate face was alive, with its curious, hard-to-read look of determination. Had only her friends considered her marriage unfortunate? Or had Julia herself discovered her mistake, tasting her bitter tears in the merciful privacy of night? What vast distances of experience Dorothea seemed to have traveled since she first saw this portrait! She felt a new companionship with it, as if it could listen and understand her gaze. This was a woman who had encountered difficulty in marriage. Then the colors seemed to deepen; the chin and lips grew fuller; light seemed to stream from the eyes and hair. The face became a man’s, smiling at her with that absorbed attention which tells a woman that even the slightest movement of her eyelids matters and will be noticed. The vivid image warmed Dorothea pleasantly. She found herself smiling. Turning away, she sat and looked up as though once more speaking to someone before her. As she continued thinking, however, the smile faded. At last she spoke aloud.
“Oh, how cruel to say that! How sad—how terrible!”

She sprang up and left the room, hurrying down the corridor, driven by an irresistible wish to see her husband and ask if she could help him. Perhaps Mr. Tucker had gone and Mr. Casaubon was alone in the library. If her husband could be glad to see her, she felt, all the morning’s darkness would disappear.
But at the top of the dark oak staircase she found Celia coming up. Below them, Mr. Brooke and Mr. Casaubon were exchanging greetings and congratulations.

“Dodo!” Celia said in her quiet, clipped way. She kissed her sister, who put both arms around her, and said nothing else. I think each shed a few secret tears before Dorothea hurried downstairs to welcome her uncle.

“No need to ask how you are, my dear,” Mr. Brooke said after kissing her forehead. “Rome has done you good, plainly—happiness, frescoes, antiquities, all that. Very pleasant to have you home. You’re an expert on art now, I suppose? Mr. Casaubon looks a little pale, though, as I’ve been telling him. Rather pale. Working hard on holiday is taking things too far. I did too much myself once.” He still held Dorothea’s hand, but turned toward her husband. “Topography, ruins, temples—I thought I’d found a clue. Then I realized where it might lead, with perhaps nothing to show for it. You can go on indefinitely with that sort of thing and get nowhere, you know.”
Dorothea also looked anxiously up at her husband. Perhaps someone seeing him after an absence could detect signs she had missed.

“Nothing to worry about, my dear,” said Mr. Brooke, noticing her expression. “Some English beef and mutton will soon set him right. Looking pale was well enough when he was sitting for that portrait of Aquinas—we received your letter just in time, you know. But Aquinas—wasn’t he a little too subtle? Does anyone actually read him?”
“He is certainly not a writer suited to shallow minds,” Mr. Casaubon replied, meeting these well-timed questions with dignified patience.
“Would you like coffee in your room, Uncle?” Dorothea intervened.
“Yes, and you must go to Celia. She has important news for you. I’ll leave her to tell it.”

With Celia sitting there in an outer dress exactly like her sister’s, the blue-green room looked far more cheerful. She examined the cameos in placid contentment as their conversation moved to other things.
“Do you think Rome is a nice place for a honeymoon?” Celia asked, with the delicate, ready blush that Dorothea was accustomed to seeing for the slightest reason.
“It wouldn’t suit everyone—not you, for instance, darling,” Dorothea answered calmly. Nobody would ever know what she thought of a honeymoon in Rome.

“Mrs. Cadwallader says it’s foolish to travel a long way just after getting married. She says people grow sick to death of each other and can’t even quarrel comfortably, as they could at home. Lady Chettam says she went to Bath.” Celia’s blush kept rising and fading, seeming
“To run back and forth with messages from the heart, like a messenger hurrying on its errands.”
This had to mean more than her usual blushes did.
“Celia! Has something happened?” Dorothea asked with all a sister’s warmth. “Is there really important news?”
“It was because you went away, Dodo. That left Sir James with only me to talk to,” said Celia, a mischievous gleam in her eyes.

“I see. It’s what I used to hope for and expect,” Dorothea said, holding her sister’s face between her hands and studying it with some anxiety. Celia’s marriage now seemed a more serious matter than before.
“It only happened three days ago,” Celia said. “Lady Chettam has been very kind.”
“And you’re happy—truly happy?”
“Yes. We’re not marrying just yet, because everything has to be prepared. And I don’t want it to happen too soon. Being engaged is lovely, I think. We’ll have the rest of our lives to be married.”
“I really believe you couldn’t choose a better husband, Kitty,” Dorothea said warmly. “Sir James is a good man, and an honorable one.”
“He’s continued work on the cottages, Dodo. When he comes, he’ll tell you all about them. Will you be pleased to see him?”
“Of course! How could you doubt it?”
“I was only afraid you might be becoming terribly learned,” said Celia. She regarded Mr. Casaubon’s learning as a sort of damp that might eventually soak into anyone nearby.
